newsitem.title: USA: Galileo passes close to Jupiter moon Europa.
newsitem.headline: Galileo passes close to Jupiter moon Europa.

text.p: The Galileo spacecraft passed within 360 miles (580 km) of Jupiter's icy moon Europa on Thursday, looking for evidence that might boost scientists' speculation that it could support some form of life.
"Everything went as planned. There was no hitch," Jane Platt, a spokeswoman at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory said.

Galileo, which was launched aboard the space shuttle Atlantis on Oct. 18, 1989, made its first pass of Europa last December, revealing remarkable details of the moon's surface, said the JPL, which manages the Galileo project for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

This week's closer flyby will look at other areas of Europa's surface, which is covered by ice and criss-crossed by dark lines. Scientists believe liquid oceans might be hidden under the icy surface of the moon and the presence of liquid would boost the odds of Europa hosting some form of life.

"On Earth, deep down in our oceans near internal vents on ocean floors, scientists have found forms of life that until very recently we didn't have any idea existed. That has increased our speculation that something similar might be going on in Europa," Galileo mission director Bob Mitchell said.
"It's purely speculation, but it's possible," he told local KTLA television.

With a diameter of 1,946 miles (3,138 km), Europa is slightly smaller than Earth's moon. Because the geometry of this latest encounter is different from the previous path, it will yield data and images of different portions of the moon.

A third Europa flyby was planned for November 1997, and JPL has asked NASA to extend the Galileo mission by two years to include eight more such flybys and an encounter with Io, one of Jupiter's other moons.
